StudentBook helps private tutors keep student contacts and tuition details in one place. It runs on your computer and uses typed commands.

StudentBook supports student contacts, optional schooling levels and guardian contacts. Each student can have multiple lessons; each lesson records a subject, weekly time slot and hourly rate, with optional mode and location. Use `lesson-add`, `lesson-edit` and `lesson-delete` to manage lessons, and `guardian-add`, `guardian-edit` and `guardian-delete` to manage a student's guardian contact. `find` can search by name or combine filters for name (`name/`), guardian (`guardian/`), school (`sch/`), schooling level, lesson subject and day; the lesson filters also apply to the weekly calendar. Changes are saved automatically.
* Add, list, edit and delete student records.
* Record an optional schooling level and guardian contact, plus multiple lessons with subjects, weekly time slots and hourly rates.
* Save records locally and reopen them later.
All five tuition features are part of the MVP. Payment processing and sending messages are out of scope. Other brainstormed ideas are backlog candidates, not promised additions.

This project uses Gradle for **build automation and dependency management**. **We recommend reading [this Gradle tutorial from se-edu/guides](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/gradle.html).**
The following commands perform common Gradle tasks.
* **`clean`**: Deletes the files created during the previous build tasks (e.g. files in the `build` folder).
* **`shadowJar`**: Uses the Shadow plugin to create the fat JAR file `build/libs/studentbook.jar`.
**`runShadow`**: Builds the application as a fat JAR, then runs it.
* **`checkstyleMain`**: Runs the code style check for the main code base.
**`checkstyleTest`**: Runs the code style check for the test code base.
* `./gradlew clean test`: Cleans the project before running all tests
* **`seed`**: Writes a data file of realistic, randomly generated students for manual and stress testing. See [Generating test data](Testing.md#generating-test-data).
For example: `./gradlew seed` writes 40 students to `data/studentbook.json`.
This project uses GitHub Actions for CI. The necessary workflow configuration files are in `.github/workflows`. No further setup is required.
As part of CI, Gradle generates JaCoCo coverage reports from the tests, and CI uploads the coverage data to Codecov. Codecov then provides information about test coverage.

The GitHub Actions build and the Codecov coverage status are separate checks. A successful Gradle build does not mean Codecov's coverage target passed. If Codecov reports a failure, inspect its report to distinguish a coverage drop from an upload or service error. Review the uncovered code and add useful tests where appropriate; a coverage-target failure does not by itself mean the build or tests failed.
To enable Codecov for forks of this project, follow the steps given in [this se-edu guide](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/codecov.html).

In addition to Gradle checks, CI runs repository-wide checks. Unlike Gradle checks, which cover files used in the build, these checks cover every repository file and enforce rules that are hard to apply on development machines, such as line-ending requirements.

Any warnings or errors will be printed out to the console.

* Checks are implemented as executable `check-*` scripts within the `.github` directory. The `run-checks.sh` script will automatically pick up and run files named as such. That is, you can add more such files if you need and the CI will do the rest.
* Check scripts should print out errors in the format `SEVERITY:FILENAME:LINE: MESSAGE`
* SEVERITY is either ERROR or WARN.
* FILENAME is the path to the file relative to the current directory.
* LINE is the line of the file where the error occurred and MESSAGE is the message explaining the error.
* Check scripts must exit with a non-zero exit code if any errors occur.
Here are the steps to create a new release from the tested team `master` branch.

1. Update the version number in this repository's [`MainApp.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-F13-4/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java) to match the planned release, e.g. `V1.3` for tag `v1.3`. Merge that change before building the release.
1. Check the merged commit with `./gradlew check` and generate its fat JAR with `./gradlew shadowJar` (Windows: `gradlew.bat`). The output is `build/libs/studentbook.jar`.

1. Copy the JAR to a clean, writable folder outside the repository. Run `java -jar studentbook.jar`, try the main student, lesson, guardian and search workflows, close the app, then reopen it and check that changes persist in `data/studentbook.json`.

1. Capture screenshots or a recording of the released app showing its main features. Write release notes that describe the changes since the previous release (for v1.3, since AB3) and include that visual evidence.

1. Tag the tested merged commit with the release version, e.g. `v1.3`. [Create a GitHub release](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/managing-releases-in-a-repository) from that tag, paste the release notes and upload the tested `studentbook.jar`.

After a valid lesson addition or edit, `LessonCommand` calls `LessonClashes.warning` with the complete active or archived
student list matching the edited student and the changed lesson's position. Search filters do not limit clash checks.
The helper excludes that lesson itself and checks every other lesson in that list.
Intervals clash when their weekdays match and each starts strictly before the other ends. Thus touching endpoints
are allowed. The warning is appended to normal success feedback; existing validation and persistence still apply.
Deleting a lesson requires no clash warning. No clash state is stored, so each warning reflects current records.
Clashing changes return `CommandResult.warning`. `MainWindow` routes these successful results to
`ResultDisplay#setWarningToUser`, which applies an amber warning style and an exclamation icon.
The next success, error or warning result replaces the previous feedback and clears its styling.

A `FollowUp` holds 1–200 characters of single-line text, trimmed, and counted in code points like note text. `Student`
keeps its outstanding follow-ups in an unmodifiable list in the order they were added; a follow-up's position in that
list is the `FOLLOW_UP_INDEX` shown in the details. Completing an item removes it, so the model has no "done" state:
every stored item is outstanding. Follow-ups belong to the student rather than the `Guardian`, so they survive
`guardian-delete` and can be recorded for a student with no guardian (for example, while waiting for contact details).

`FollowUpCommand` resolves the student from the current filtered list, rejects a follow-up index past the end, and
rejects text that matches another of the student's items ignoring case (an item may be edited to change only its
case). It then replaces the student with a copy whose follow-ups have changed. The success message includes the
item's text, so a wrong index on `followup-done` is visible straight away.
`followups` (`FollowUpListCommand`) sets the student filter to active (not archived) students with at least one
item, matching `list`, which hides archived students. It also resets the lesson filter.
Because the filtered list re-applies its predicate after `Model#setPerson`, completing a student's last item while
this filter is active removes the student from the list and renumbers the students after them. `FollowUpCommand`
therefore opens the student's details at the student's new position, and opens none if the student is no longer shown,
so the details never show the wrong student.

1. **Compatibility.** Run on Windows, macOS and Linux with Java `25`, on systems supported by the bundled JavaFX runtime.

* **StudentBook**: The desktop app for managing student records.
* **Independent private tutor**: A tutor who manages students and lessons without administrative staff.
* **Student record**: One student's contact details, school, schooling level, guardian contact, lessons and dated progress notes.
* **Guardian contact**: The name and phone number of the adult responsible for a student. The first version allows one optional guardian per student. A recorded guardian needs both fields.
* **Schooling level**: The student's stage of primary or secondary education, such as Primary 5 or Secondary 3.
* **Subject**: An academic subject taught by the tutor to a student, such as Mathematics or English.
* **Lesson**: One recurring arrangement for a student: a subject, a weekly slot and an hourly rate, with an optional location and mode. A student can have many lessons.
* **Recurring lesson slot**: A lesson's weekly day, start time and end time on a single day.
* **Lesson mode**: Whether a lesson is physical or virtual.
* **Hourly rate**: The agreed SGD amount per hour for a lesson, stored as `BigDecimal`. It does not calculate fees or process payments.
* **Progress note**: A dated note recording a student's learning progress or observations from a lesson.
* **Guardian follow-up item**: A recorded action the tutor needs to carry out for a guardian, such as providing an update. An outstanding item has not yet been marked complete.
* **Displayed index**: The number beside a student in the current list. It can change when the list changes, so it is not a permanent student ID.
* **Local storage**: Files on the tutor's computer that keep records between launches.
* **Private contact detail**: A student or guardian's phone number, email address, or other contact information intended for the tutor's use rather than public sharing.

The `seed` Gradle task writes a StudentBook data file filled with realistic Singapore tuition students: local names, HDB addresses, primary to JC levels and adult learners, schools that fit each level, guardians, siblings who share a guardian and address, weekly lessons with typical subjects, slots, rates, locations and modes, and a few progress notes, guardian follow-ups and archived students. It builds students from the real model classes and saves them through `JsonAddressBookStorage`, so every generated file is one the app can load. The generator is `seedu.address.testutil.StudentBookSeeder`.
Run it with no arguments to write 40 students to `data/studentbook.json`:
To change the defaults, pass options through `--args`, e.g. `./gradlew seed --args="--students 500 --force"`:
`--students N` | Number of random students, at most 1376 (the number of distinct names the generator can make). Try 500 for stress testing. | `40`
`--seed S` | Random seed. The same seed always gives the same file. | `2103`
`--out FILE` | File to write, relative to the repository root. | `data/studentbook.json`
`--force` | Replace `FILE` if it already exists. Without it, the task refuses and leaves the file unchanged, so it never wipes your own data by accident. |
`--edge-cases` | Also add fixed students for boundary testing (see below). The random students are unchanged. |
The task prints the number of students, lessons and overlapping lesson pairs it wrote. Since the default output is the file the app loads, `./gradlew run` then opens the generated data.
`--edge-cases` adds these fixed students after the random ones:
* `Alex Tan` and `alex tan`, whose names differ only in letter case.
* A student whose name, address, tags, school, level, subject, location, progress note and follow-up are at or near their length limits.
* Back-to-back lessons that touch but do not overlap (Monday and Friday).
* A partial overlap, a lesson contained in another, and two lessons in exactly the same slot (Wednesday and Thursday).
* A lesson whose location is a full Zoom link.
* A student with no lessons, and a student with no lessons, guardian, level or school.
* An archived student, who is hidden from the default list.

* **This week:** The calendar shows Monday to Sunday of the current week, with today's date circled and a red line at the current time. Each lesson shows the student, the time, and then its number, level and subject, such as `#3.1 · Sec 3 · A-Math`. The number means student `3`, lesson `1`, so `lesson-edit 3 1` changes that lesson. The app saves automatically after each successfully executed command. Schools, schooling levels, guardian contacts and lessons are saved with the contact details. [SE-EDU review guidance](https://se-education.org/guides/guidelines/PRs-reviewing.html).

Coverage warnings can be an informed exception when a part is unsuitable for automated testing or tests are deliberately deferred. Codecov targets can be adjusted; Codecov itself is not graded. This is not a blanket reason to ignore compilation failures, broken behavior, or style violations. Restore a useful passing CI state promptly. Occasional failures do not automatically incur a direct penalty; prolonged failures remove regression protection and can reveal separately penalized problems.

If local tests pass but a PR fails, compare OS behavior and reproduce the PR's merge with current `master`. PR CI tests the proposed combined state, not necessarily the exact standalone branch tested locally. If `master` changed after CI passed, synchronize and rerun before merging. File case, separators, locale/time assumptions, and platform-sensitive behavior deserve attention; do not assume a filesystem's case sensitivity solely from its OS name.

The course requires SE-EDU's **basic and intermediate Java rules**. Advanced Java rules, the Markdown guide, and Google's documentation style are optional. [Course conventions](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/standardsAndConventions.html).

Java review reminders: use meaningful English names, lower-case packages, PascalCase types, camelCase members, uppercase underscore-separated constants, Boolean-sounding predicates, and plural collection names. Use four-space indentation, eight extra spaces for continuations, and a 120-character hard limit (110 preferred). Use braces, consistent explicit imports, narrow variable scope, and encapsulated fields. Keep layout and whitespace consistent. Document classes and public methods; exemptions include ordinary accessors, tests, and overrides whose inherited contract applies unchanged. Javadoc opens on its own line, starts a method summary with a third-person verb such as "Returns," and sits immediately above the declaration. Include useful parameter/return/exception details, with all parameters documented or none under the standard's omission rule. Use American English. [Complete Java standard](https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/java/intermediate.html).

Every commit needs an imperative, initially capitalized subject without a final period. Aim for 50 characters, with 72 as the hard limit; a meaningful scope/category prefix is allowed. A body is optional for this course. If present, separate it with a blank line, wrap at 72 characters, and use paragraphs explaining the change and its reason. More elaborate conventions are optional. [Git conventions](https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/git.html).

Each member should contribute functional code and some automated tests, plus their own UG/DG updates. There is **no minimum coverage percentage** and no requirement to automate GUI testing. A useful strategy checks ordinary flows, invalid inputs, boundary cases, interactions, persistence, and regressions introduced by a change.

Early iterations may preserve existing tests without immediately adding new ones. Temporary disabling during volatile development or a draft PR is discussed as an option, with explicit risks: hidden regressions, accumulating test debt, and forgotten re-enablement. By final assessment, weak tests can cost marks through escaped bugs and lack of evidence of testing skill.

## Phase 1: scope, report format, and selection

Source inspection can help testing, but a code-quality concern needs an observable in-scope defect to become a PE report. Configuration/data files matter through supported behavior, including documented manual editing. Terminal output is lower-priority but can be a bug when misleading or alarming. Start with the manual-test appendix and expand into exploratory, system, and acceptance testing.

Each issue must be self-contained and report **one bug**. Include a specific title, setup/version/environment where relevant, reproducible steps, actual and expected results, and evidence of user impact. Put everything needed in the description: Phase 1 comments are not processed as part of the report. Do not use cross-issue links or sub-issues to bundle reports; IDs can change during transfer. Escape angle-bracket placeholders or put them in code formatting so GitHub does not hide them as HTML.
Use exactly one type and one severity label:
| `type.FunctionalityBug` | Implemented behavior does not work as it should |
| `type.FeatureFlaw` | A design choice or missing capability impairs the target user's task |
| `type.DocumentationBug` | Incorrect, missing, confusing, or badly presented UG/DG information |
| `severity.VeryLow` | Cosmetic/minor presentation issue without meaningful operational disruption |
| `severity.Low` | Minor issue or rare inconvenience; limited interference with normal work |
| `severity.Medium` | Meaningful occasional inconvenience, while the product can still be used |
| `severity.High` | Makes the product almost unusable for most intended users |

Do not bundle numerous cosmetic defects under an extremely broad issue to evade the limit. If several distinct bugs are combined, developers may select one and discard the others. A valid defect remains valid even if the tester suggests the wrong fix or chooses the wrong type label.

Choose exactly one response label and ensure type/severity are correct even when disputing the report:
| `response.Accepted` | It is a valid defect that should be addressed in the current product |
| `response.NotInScope` | It is a valid improvement, but justifiably lower-priority than the work delivered |
| `response.NotApplicable` | The alleged problem is not a valid defect; behavior is correct or the claim is mistaken |
| `response.CannotReproduce` | Reasonable repeated attempts with the available information cannot reproduce it |
| `response.IssueUnclear` | The report lacks enough understandable information to determine the issue |

Missing or multiple response labels default to Accepted. Do not confuse NotInScope with NotApplicable: the former acknowledges a valid potential improvement. Do not reject a real defect for a wrong label or incorrect proposed remedy; correct the label and explain which remedy is appropriate. Reporters cannot participate in an informal clarification conversation during this anonymous phase, so do not rely on asking questions in ordinary comments.

Put the developer explanation in **one comment starting with `# T`**, at most **500 words**. The latest matching comment is used. A comment is required when lowering severity, choosing a non-Accepted response, marking a duplicate, or changing type. Accepting entirely unchanged needs no justification. A type change needs the response comment but does not itself require a justification under the current instructions. Explain all disputed decisions clearly, using titles rather than unstable cross-repository issue numbers.

Unjustified rejection or downgrading is weak evidence if challenged. Moderators choose between supported positions; do not start with an exaggerated bargaining position in the hope of meeting halfway. Use a separate `# U` comment only for unprofessional conduct, not for an inaccurate or unpersuasive report.

Use GitHub **sub-issues**: make duplicate reports children of one representative original report. Keep the structure flat; do not create chains of duplicates. The original's response/type/severity/assignees control the children. Each child's `# T` explanation must state why it is a duplicate. The tester receives both relevant explanations, so put any inherited severity reduction's rationale where it will be visible.

Reports are duplicates when they concern the same defect or a common underlying problem that cannot be fixed independently. Similar symptoms alone are insufficient. Two unrelated typos that can be corrected independently are not automatically duplicates. If the duplicate classification is overturned, the inherited classification can still matter under the stated process, so choose and justify it carefully.

Recommended team process: set an internal responsibility-assignment deadline, assign remaining reports by agreement, draft responses, and have teammates check them before the external deadline. Accurate fair responses matter more than reducing the accepted count.

Wait for the official announcement before acting; seeing script comments appear does not mean the transfer is finished. Responses are copied back to the tester's private repository. Read the report's listed aspects that may be challenged. The permitted objections are response, lowered severity, and duplicate status; **bug type is not an objection category**.
If you agree, no counter-response is needed. Otherwise, add a separate comment for each disputed aspect, **at most 500 words each**, starting with the exact applicable heading:

For `# R`, explicitly say if the requested outcome is NotInScope; otherwise Accepted is assumed. Additional evidence may be provided, but it carries less weight than information included in the original report, especially if the developer could not reasonably infer it. Explain why the response is wrong instead of merely repeating the report.

Do not change the original title/body/labels, create/edit/delete repository labels, or close issues in this phase. Reopen an accidentally closed issue. Edit the existing objection before the deadline rather than creating multiple versions. No objection means agreement; optional agreement checkboxes do not replace a required objection.

To withdraw an objection, delete it or remove its special heading. Hiding it or checking an agreement box does **not** retract it. There is little value in disputing severity/duplicate status after agreeing to a response that earns no bug credit. NotInScope is different: severity still affects the value of the accepted improvement and the accuracy calculation.

The current rules offer an accuracy amnesty for agreeing with the developer's response, not for an incorrect original severity. An unsuccessful objection can reduce accuracy, particularly when better information was available. Correct final response/severity judgments can improve credit; published bonus percentages are indicative and should be reread before relying on them.

Tutors adjudicate disputes using the report, developer explanation, and tester objection. Students normally take no further action. Staff will not pre-decide whether a proposed report is a bug or assign its severity during the assessment; those are assessed judgments. General procedural questions can go through the designated channel with relevant context.
## Triage principles for design and implementation
Read the full [PE triage guidelines](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/tp-pe.html) for a contested case. These points should also guide development before PE:
- **Inherited defects:** AB3 behavior is not automatically exempt. The team owns its delivered product.

- **Reproduction:** make a reasonable attempt to understand the issue even if steps are imperfect but screenshots/context reveal it. OS-specific defects are valid on supported systems; affected reach can influence severity. A transferred broken image may need staff assistance rather than instant rejection.

- **Scope:** NotInScope needs a credible priority/resource argument relative to work already done. A known limitation or coming-soon note is evidence, not immunity. Essential usability or an obviously better design achievable at similar effort is difficult to defer credibly. If equally persuasive subjective design arguments remain, the course's feature-design FAQ favors the developer.

- **Long/extreme inputs:** deliberate sabotage alone can fall outside scope, but ordinary mistakes must not crash the app, corrupt data, or make it unusable. Apply the same principle to numeric overflow. Reasonable length limits are allowed; limits must fit actual users. Clipping can be cosmetic or serious depending on information lost.

- **Validation:** accepting useful real-world inputs often matters more than enforcing a programmer's narrow format. Warn rather than block when flexibility is safe; handle harmful invalid input properly. A parser delimiter is not by itself a sufficient reason to exclude common legitimate names without considering impact.

- **Duplicates and search:** case/whitespace variants can represent the same entity. Warn about near matches where appropriate, allow sensible user choice, and explain detection limits. Case sensitivity should reflect the represented domain. Search should help the user recover likely results; the guideline's OR-versus-AND example is context-specific, not a command to rewrite every search.

- **Commands:** optimize frequent tasks for fast typing with memorable syntax; unnecessary case sensitivity, long keywords, or awkward characters can be feature flaws. Useful short aliases plus longer memorable forms can help.

- **Errors:** identify the actual problem and remedy where feasible. A generic message can be inadequate even when technically true. Distinguish invalid values from malformed input, or give an accurate combined message where further differentiation is justifiably lower-priority.
- **Manual data editing:** support at least AB3's promise that correctly edited files work. Stronger UG promises must be met. The human-editable storage constraint still applies.

- **Undocumented behavior:** hidden unreleased work may be outside the released scope if users are unlikely to encounter it. An exposed unfinished feature, or a useful non-obvious feature with missing instructions, can be a bug. Obvious intuitive behavior need not always have a lengthy UG entry.

Broken links can be Low or Medium depending on their effect. Formatting, spacing, inconsistent alignment, or unreadable diagrams can be bugs even if a determined reader could work around them; minor presentation issues are usually VeryLow. An obvious typo, including text in the UI, is normally a VeryLow documentation bug, while an inconsequential grammatical preference may be NotInScope.

UML must use correct relevant course notation. Harmless extra tool decorations are different from misleading notation. Consistent omission of optional notation can be acceptable; intentional abstraction should be clear, whereas accidental omissions that misrepresent the design are defects. Do not assume zooming excuses tiny text. Incorrect requirements, missing important interaction cases, and unrealistic/unmet NFR claims can also be documentation defects or design flaws depending on what needs changing.

A UG need not contain every validation corner case when the product informs the user adequately. Conversely, claims must match behavior and important limitations must be disclosed. Choose bug type by the needed correction: change behavior/design for a product defect, or correct the guide for a documentation error. Neither a misleading guide nor a poor design is excused merely because the two agree.

The grading checklist also flags too few or too many visuals/examples, visuals disconnected from the explanation, repetitive content, unexplained audience-specific jargon, and descriptions that are too short or unnecessarily long. DG-specific risks include non-intuitive architecture symbols, indiscriminate double-headed arrows, low-level detail in an architecture view, an unsuitable diagram type, non-UML diagrams where UML would serve equally well, excessive code extracts, mismatched user-story parts, missing important stories/use cases, bad step numbering, unnecessary UI details in use cases, missing extensions, and vague or implausible NFRs. Check whether each glossary entry actually helps the intended reader.

Activity diagrams model workflows: a user's process, or the control flow of an algorithm. They are UML's version of flow charts. In the DG they suit command workflows with branches or loops, such as `CommitActivityDiagram.puml`.

Verify every diagram by looking at it: render, open the PNG, check notation, layout and match with the code, then commit the PNG with the `.puml`. See the [README steps](README.md#look-at-every-diagram-you-make).
- Control flow: line with an arrowhead. The arrowhead style doesn't matter.
- Start node: filled circle. End node: filled circle inside a ring. They are not interchangeable.
- Branch node: diamond with several outgoing flows. Each outgoing flow carries a guard in square brackets, and exactly one guard is true at any time.
- Merge node: diamond where alternate paths rejoin.

- Fork and join: a bar. A fork starts parallel paths; a join ends them. Every path from a fork ends at the same join, and all paths finish before the flow continues. Actions in parallel paths may interleave, but each path keeps its own order.
- Omit the merge node when that causes no ambiguity.
- Several flows may leave the same corner of a branch diamond.
- Omit `[else]` when all other paths have guards.
- Rake: a small rake symbol inside an action means the action is detailed in a separate activity diagram.
- Swimlanes: vertical partitions headed by who does each action.
## Correct and incorrect, from the course's exercise answers
- One action between start and end is fine.
- More than two alternate paths, paths that branch again, paths that rejoin other branches, and a branch looping back to its own diamond are all fine.

- Wrong: swapped start and end symbols; square-cornered actions; double-headed arrows; overlapping guards such as `[x >= 5]` and `[x <= 5]`; guards without square brackets; parallel paths that end in different joins or never reach a join.
- Put guards on the outgoing flows. A branch diamond holds no text.
- Keep one level of detail per diagram and rake out the rest.
- Don't let two guards be true at once.
- Don't merge parallel paths with a diamond; end them with a join bar.
- Use the new syntax with `start` and `stop`. `stop` draws the course's end node. `end` draws a circled X (flow final), which the course doesn't teach.

Class diagrams show the structure of an OO solution, not its behaviour. The course uses them for detailed design inside a component (the DG's Logic, Model and Storage diagrams) and, in a lighter form, for domain models.

Verify every diagram by looking at it: render, open the PNG, check notation, layout and match with the code, then commit the PNG with the `.puml`. See the [README steps](README.md#look-at-every-diagram-you-make).
- Three compartments: name, attributes, operations. Attributes always sit above operations.
- Attribute format `visibility name: type = default-value`. Operation format `visibility name(parameter-list): return-type`.
- All attributes go in one compartment; all operations in one compartment.
- Either compartment may be omitted or left empty. Members irrelevant to the diagram's purpose may be left out.
- Visibility: `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected, `~` package private. No symbol means unspecified.
- Generic classes show the type parameter in a small dashed box on the top-right corner of the class box.
- Solid line between the two classes.

- Navigability is an arrowhead on that line. The arrowhead is open (lined), not a filled triangle. `Logic --> Minefield` means a Logic object holds a reference to its Minefield. Arrowheads at both ends mean bidirectional, meaning both objects point to each other for the same link. Two separate one-way associations in opposite directions are not a bidirectional association.
- Multiplicity sits at the end of the line next to the class it counts: `0..1`, `1`, `*`, `n..m` (`1..*`, `2..5`). No multiplicity means unspecified.

- Role names also sit at the end of the line next to the class playing the role. Roles usually match the field name in code (`Man` has a field `wife`, so the role at the `Woman` end is `wife`). They are optional, but useful for telling apart several associations between the same two classes.
- An association label sits mid-line and describes the meaning. A small arrowhead next to it shows which way to read it (`Admin uses ▶ Student`).

- An association may instead be written as an attribute: `name: type [multiplicity] = default`, for example `squares: Square[100]`. Show each association as a line or an attribute, never both. The course prefers the line because it is easier to spot. ([W8.2c](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/book/uml/classDiagrams/associationsAsAttributes/what/))
- Inheritance: solid line with a triangle at the parent. Filled or hollow does not matter, though hollow is typical.
- Interface: class box with `<<interface>>` above the name. Implementing it is drawn like inheritance but with a dashed line.
- Abstract class or method: `{abstract}` (preferred) or italics.
- Enumeration: `<<enumeration>>` above the name, values listed in the compartment below.

- Composition: filled diamond at the whole. Means the part cannot exist without the whole and there are no cycles. Deleting parts along with the whole is not enough on its own; the part must be an integral part of the whole at the concept level.
- Aggregation: hollow diamond. The course quotes Fowler's advice to leave it out because it adds confusion, and its exercise answer marks it as the symbol not to use.

- Dependency: dashed arrow from the class that depends to the class depended on. Use it only for a dependency the diagram doesn't already show. An association or inheritance already implies one. Typical cases are using another class's static member, or receiving an object as a parameter without keeping it.
- Generics with inheritance: `Goo extends Foo<String>` is drawn as a separate `Foo` box bound to `String`, with a dashed arrow to `Foo<T>`, optionally labelled `<<bind>>` and `<T -> String>`.

- Association class: a normal class joined by a dashed line to the middle of an association. It holds data about the link itself, like a `Marriage` date between `Man` and `Woman`. A property of only one end is not an association class: the course answer rejects `Mileage` on the `Driver` to `Car` link. ([W8.2e](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/book/oop/associations/associationClasses/))
- A note is a box with a folded corner, attached by a dashed line or left free-standing.
- A constraint goes inside a note in curly braces, written in natural language or OCL.
- `<<role/purpose>>` above a class name optionally marks the role it plays, such as `<<Singleton>>` or `<<Facade>>`.

An object diagram is a snapshot of objects and their links at one moment. It is an instance of a class diagram. In the DG it suits state snapshots, such as the undo/redo history diagrams `UndoRedoState0.puml` to `UndoRedoState5.puml`.

- Object box header `objectName:ClassName`, underlined. `:ClassName` for an unnamed object.
- Attributes as `attribute = value`, for example `size = 3`. No visibility, no type.
- Leave out class-level attributes; they belong to the class.
- The attributes compartment may be omitted. The operations compartment is always omitted.
- A link is a solid line. Navigability arrowheads are allowed.
- No multiplicities: each line links exactly one object to one other.
- No inheritance lines, abstract classes, interfaces or dependencies.

- Association labels or roles only when needed to tell links apart. The course example: if a `Student` links to two `Degree` objects through `major` and `minor` associations, a link without a role is ambiguous.

- For a subclass instance, show one object, typed as the child or the parent class. Never draw both a `Person` object and an `Employee` object for the same person. Using the parent type is fine if the subclass doesn't matter to the reader.
- Several object diagrams can come from one class diagram.
- Check that every link is allowed by the class diagram's multiplicities.
- Name objects when the text refers to them (`ab0:AddressBook`).
- Don't show operations, multiplicities, types or visibility.
- Don't leave object names un-underlined. That is the main visual difference from a class box, and from a sequence diagram participant.
- PlantUML does not underline object names. Write them as `object "<u>alice:Student</u>" as alice`. `UndoRedoState1.puml` does the same with `class State1 as "<u>ab0:AddressBook</u>"`.

A sequence diagram shows how entities interact in one scenario: components responding to a user action, or objects inside a component handling one method call. In the DG it is the main way to explain how a command runs.

Verify every diagram by looking at it: render, open the PNG, check notation, layout and match with the code, then commit the PNG with the `.puml`. See the [README steps](README.md#look-at-every-diagram-you-make).
- Entities are actors (stick figures) or instances (boxes). Time runs downwards.
- A participant is `:TextUi` for an unnamed instance, or `name:Class` to tell two instances apart. Names are not underlined, unlike object diagrams.
- Lifeline: dashed vertical line while the instance exists.
- Method call: solid arrow with a filled arrowhead, labelled with the operation. Return: dashed arrow, optionally labelled with the returned value.
- Lined (open) arrowheads mean asynchronous calls. The course treats them as out of scope, so every call uses a filled head.
- Activation bar: the period the method runs. It starts when the call arrives and ends when the method returns.
- Object creation: the constructor arrow ends at the side of the new object's box, which sits at the height of the call. The constructor's activation bar hangs below the box.

- Minimal notation: activation bars and return arrows may be dropped if that loses nothing; informal labels such as `get minefield info` are allowed when exact calls don't matter; `foo(...)` hides parameters.
- Deletion: the lifeline ends in an X. In Java this marks where the object stops being referenced and can be garbage-collected.

- Self-invocation: an arrow from the object's bar back to itself, with a second bar stacked on the first. Callbacks to the caller (`Chapter#getText()` calling back `Book#getAuthor()`) also stack a bar on the caller's bar.

- Unroll chained calls first. `new Book().add(new Chapter())` becomes three arrows: create `b:Book`, create `c:Chapter`, then `add(c)`. `person.getAddress().printStreet()` becomes two calls on two participants.
- `alt` frame with `[guard]` partitions separated by dashed lines. At most one partition runs; none running is fine.
- Static method: the call goes to the class itself, shown as a participant labelled `<<class>>` above the class name, such as `<<class>> Person`.
- An object created and not stored (`new Quote().print()`) can be shown deleted soon after its last call. (W6.1b exercise hint.)
- `par` frame: partitions run in parallel. In Java this implies multithreading, so StudentBook will rarely need it.
- `ref` frame: a named box spanning the participants involved, standing in for an interaction drawn as a separate diagram. The separate diagram is framed with `sd` and the same name.
- Activation bar too long: starting before the call arrives, or continuing after the return.
- Broken activation bar: a gap in the middle of one method's execution.

- Start with `[-> X : method(args)` for a call arriving from outside the diagram, and end with `[<-- X`.

- Use `ref` frames to split long flows, and omit routine self-calls and getters that don't help.
- Don't use `->>`. It draws the lined arrowhead, which means asynchronous.
- Don't use any frame keyword other than `loop`, `alt`, `opt`, `par`, `ref` and `sd`.
- Don't draw a chained call as one arrow.

- `->` gives the filled head the course wants; `-->` gives the dashed return.

- Activation bars are manual. Put `activate X` right after the call arrow and `deactivate X` right after the return arrow. A late `activate` makes the bar start after the call; a `deactivate` followed by more calls breaks the bar.
- `create X` before the constructor arrow makes the arrow land on the box, matching the course.
- `destroy X` draws the X. Our diagrams add `X -[hidden]-> Caller` first so the X sits below the last bar (see `DeleteSequenceDiagram.puml`).
- PlantUML wraps frame guards in brackets itself. Write `alt index is valid`, `else else`, `loop each tag`. Writing `alt [index is valid]` gives double brackets.

A use case diagram is a visual table of contents for a system's use cases. The course teaches it alongside textual use cases in Week 7, and treats the textual form as where the detail lives. The DG's use cases are textual; add a diagram only if it helps a reader.

- Use case: oval. Actor: stick figure, connected to its use cases by plain lines. The course examples draw a system boundary box with the system's name.
- An actor is a role, not a person. One person can play several roles; many people can share one.
- Extension: dashed arrow labelled `<<extend>>`, pointing from the extension to the use case it extends.
- Inclusion: dashed arrow labelled `<<include>>`, pointing from the including use case to the included one. That is the opposite direction to `<<extend>>`.
- Actor generalisation: the inheritance triangle between actors. The child actor can do everything the parent can.
- Keep it brief and leave details to the textual use cases.
- Keep use cases at one level of detail.
- Show only use cases that involve an external actor.
- Don't use `System` as an actor. The course mentions the practice and recommends against it.
- Don't add low-level use cases to the diagram just because the requirements mention them. The course's ticket machine answer keeps those details in the descriptions.

- `A ..> B : <<include>>` and `Ext .> Base : <<extend>>` give dashed arrows with the right direction.
